experiences.name: Northern Lights Hunting Tour
experiences.description: Join a guided evening tour away from Reykjavik's light pollution to witness the aurora borealis dancing across the sky. Expert guides use real-time forecasts to find the best viewing spots, and you'll learn about the science behind this natural phenomenon while capturing stunning photographs.

experiences.name: Blue Lagoon Geothermal Spa
experiences.description: Soak in the world-famous milky-blue geothermal waters rich in silica and minerals. Enjoy in-water massages, silica mud masks, and swim-up bars while surrounded by dramatic lava fields. Book the Comfort package for access to the main lagoon, towel rental, and one silica mud mask.

experiences.name: Snorkeling or Diving in Silfra Fissure
experiences.description: Snorkel or dive between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates in crystal-clear glacial water with visibility up to 100 meters. The surreal blue and green hues of the water make this one of the most unique natural experiences on Earth, guided by certified instructors.

experiences.name: Secret Lagoon Natural Hot Spring
experiences.description: Relax in Iceland's oldest swimming pool, a naturally heated geothermal pool surrounded by bubbling hot springs and a small geyser that erupts every few minutes. Far less crowded than the Blue Lagoon, this authentic experience offers a peaceful soak amid stunning Icelandic countryside.

experiences.name: Skaftafell Glacier Hike on Vatnajökull
experiences.description: Strap on crampons and hike across Europe's largest glacier with an expert guide. Explore stunning ice formations, deep blue crevasses, and ash layers from ancient volcanic eruptions. The hike offers breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding black sand plains and mountain peaks.

trip_options.title: Budget Explorer - Iceland
trip_options.description: Save money without sacrificing the experience. Perfect for travelers who value authentic local experiences over luxury.

day_by_day.morning: Arrive at Keflavik International Airport at 06:10. Clear customs and collect luggage. Take the Flybus or a budget shuttle to Reykjavik BSI terminal, then arrange onward travel north toward Siglufjörður. The drive is approximately 4-5 hours via Route 1 and the Héðinsfjörður tunnel. Rest and recover from the flight during the journey.
day_by_day.afternoon: Arrive in Siglufjörður in the early afternoon. Check in early if possible at Hotel Siglunes on Lækjargata 10, or store luggage and take a gentle walk along the harbour front to get oriented. Siglufjörður is a charming small fishing town nestled in a dramatic fjord — explore the colourful wooden houses and the quiet harbour area.
day_by_day.evening: Settle into the hotel and rest after the long travel day. As darkness falls (which comes early in January), step outside or find a dark spot near the harbour to watch for the Northern Lights — January is prime aurora season in Iceland. Dress in all your warmest layers.

meals.breakfast: Grab a snack or coffee at Keflavik Airport before departure — budget around 1,500–2,000 ISK for a pastry and coffee.
meals.lunch: Pack sandwiches or snacks from a Reykjavik Bonus or Krónan supermarket during your transit stop to save money on the road.
meals.dinner: Kaffi Rauðka in Siglufjörður — a cosy local café and restaurant offering hearty Icelandic soups and fish dishes. Budget around 2,500–3,500 ISK for a main course.

day_by_day.notes: January days in Siglufjörður are very short — expect only about 4–5 hours of daylight. The Héðinsfjörður tunnel (opened 2010) connects Siglufjörður to Ólafsfjörður and makes access much easier. Check road conditions on road.is before driving as mountain roads can be icy or closed in January.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Herring Era Museum (Síldarminjasafnið) — one of Iceland's most celebrated regional museums, winner of the Council of Europe Museum Prize. It tells the fascinating story of the herring boom that made Siglufjörður prosperous. Entry is around 2,200 ISK. Note: confirm winter opening hours in advance as they may be limited.
day_by_day.afternoon: Walk the Siglufjörður town trail — a self-guided loop around the town taking in the old fish factory ruins, the church, and the scenic fjord views. The surrounding mountains are dramatic even in winter. If conditions allow, hike a short distance up the hillside above town for panoramic views of the fjord below.
day_by_day.evening: Northern Lights hunt from the hillside above Siglufjörður or along the fjord road away from town lights. The low light pollution in this remote area makes it excellent for aurora viewing. Check the Icelandic Met Office aurora forecast at en.vedur.is before heading out.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered at the hotel — pick up bread, skyr, eggs and fruit from the local Samkaup-Strax convenience store in Siglufjörður.
meals.lunch: Packed lunch from supermarket supplies — skyr, rye bread with smoked salmon or cheese, and fruit. Eat at the museum café if open.
meals.dinner: Cook a simple meal in the hotel if kitchen facilities are available, or return to Kaffi Rauðka for their fish soup — a warming and affordable option at around 1,800–2,200 ISK.

day_by_day.notes: The Herring Era Museum may have reduced winter hours — call ahead or check online. Stock up on groceries at the Samkaup-Strax store in town as options are limited and eating out every meal will strain a budget.

day_by_day.morning: Day trip to Ólafsfjörður via the Héðinsfjörður tunnel (about 20 minutes drive). Explore this equally charming small fishing village. Walk along the harbour and admire the mountain scenery surrounding the town — the peaks here are particularly dramatic in winter snow.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive back through the tunnel and continue to Dalvík, a slightly larger town about 45 minutes from Siglufjörður. Visit the Hvoll Museum which includes a quirky exhibit about the tallest man in Iceland. Walk along the Dalvík waterfront and enjoy views across Eyjafjörður toward Akureyri.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Siglufjörður before dark. Spend the evening watching for Northern Lights from the hotel or a dark spot along the fjord. If skies are clear, this is one of the best possible locations in Iceland for aurora viewing due to minimal light pollution.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered — skyr with granola, coffee, and toast at the hotel.
meals.lunch: Grab a hot dog (pylsa) from a petrol station in Dalvík — Iceland's iconic budget snack at around 500–700 ISK each.
meals.dinner: Self-catered dinner at the hotel — pasta with canned fish or a simple stew using ingredients from the local store. Budget around 1,000–1,500 ISK for ingredients.

day_by_day.notes: Fuel up the car in Dalvík or Ólafsfjörður as petrol stations in Siglufjörður may have limited hours. Always check road.is for tunnel and road conditions before driving in January.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Akureyri — Iceland's second largest city, about 1 hour from Siglufjörður via Dalvík and Route 82/1. Arrive and explore the compact city centre. Visit the iconic Akureyrarkirkja church perched on the hill above town — free entry and stunning architecture with beautiful stained glass windows.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore Akureyri's main shopping street, Hafnarstræti, and browse the local shops. Visit the Akureyri Art Museum (Listasafnið á Akureyri) for a budget-friendly cultural experience — entry around 1,500 ISK. Walk along the waterfront and enjoy views of Eyjafjörður, Iceland's longest fjord.
day_by_day.evening: Visit the Akureyri Swimming Pool (Sundlaug Akureyrar) — a fantastic budget activity at around 1,000–1,200 ISK entry. The outdoor hot pots are perfect for soaking while watching for Northern Lights on a clear evening. Return to Siglufjörður after your swim.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered at the hotel before departure.
meals.lunch: Akureyri has a Bonus supermarket — pick up supplies and eat a packed lunch, or try Bautinn restaurant for affordable traditional Icelandic food (soup of the day around 1,800 ISK).
meals.dinner: Strikið restaurant in Akureyri offers a good value lunch menu that sometimes extends to early evening, or try Greifinn for affordable pizza and pasta before the drive back. Budget 2,500–3,500 ISK.

day_by_day.notes: Akureyri is the main hub for the north — stock up on groceries at Bonus (Iceland's cheapest supermarket chain) to save significantly on food costs for the coming days. The drive back to Siglufjörður in the dark requires care on icy roads.

day_by_day.morning: Drive the Diamond Circle route — start with Goðafoss waterfall, about 45 minutes east of Akureyri on Route 1. This spectacular waterfall is one of Iceland's most beautiful and is free to visit. The name means 'Waterfall of the Gods' — in 1000 AD, a chieftain threw his Norse idols into it after Iceland adopted Christianity.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue to Lake Mývatn, about 1 hour from Goðafoss. Visit the Námaskarð geothermal area (Hverir) — a surreal landscape of bubbling mud pots, steaming fumaroles and sulphur deposits. Completely free to visit and utterly otherworldly. Also explore the Mývatn lava fields (Dimmuborgir) — free walking trails through dramatic lava formations.
day_by_day.evening: Visit the Mývatn Nature Baths (Jarðböðin við Mývatn) — a more affordable alternative to the Blue Lagoon at around 5,500 ISK entry. Soak in the geothermal lagoon surrounded by volcanic landscape. Then drive back to Siglufjörður (about 1.5 hours). Watch for Northern Lights on the return journey.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered early breakfast before the long day trip.
meals.lunch: Packed lunch from Bonus supplies eaten at Goðafoss or Mývatn — save money by avoiding the tourist cafés.
meals.dinner: Gamli Bærinn café near Mývatn for a warming bowl of lamb soup before the drive back, or self-cater on return. Budget 1,800–2,500 ISK if eating out.

day_by_day.notes: This is a long day — approximately 200km of driving round trip from Siglufjörður. Start early to make the most of the limited daylight hours. The Mývatn Nature Baths are significantly cheaper than the Blue Lagoon and equally beautiful. Dress in waterproof layers for the geothermal areas.

day_by_day.morning: Rest and recovery day in Siglufjörður. Sleep in and enjoy a leisurely morning. Take a slow walk around the town in the morning light — in January the golden hour lasts most of the day, creating beautiful photography conditions. Visit the small local church and explore the quieter back streets.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the area around Siglufjörður on foot. Walk along the fjord road south of town for views back toward the town with the mountains behind. Look for Arctic birds along the shoreline — Iceland in winter hosts various seabirds. The dramatic snow-covered peaks surrounding the fjord are spectacular on clear days.
day_by_day.evening: Northern Lights evening — this is a dedicated aurora hunt night. Drive a few kilometres out of town along the fjord road to escape any light pollution. Bring a thermos of hot chocolate, warm blankets, and a tripod if you have a camera. The forecast from en.vedur.is will indicate the best chances.

meals.breakfast: Leisurely self-catered breakfast — scrambled eggs, toast, skyr and coffee.
meals.lunch: Kaffi Rauðka for a treat — their fish soup or lamb soup is warming and reasonably priced at around 1,800–2,200 ISK.
meals.dinner: Self-catered dinner — cook a hearty meal using Icelandic lamb mince (available at Samkaup-Strax) for a traditional kjötsúpa (lamb soup) experience at home.

day_by_day.notes: Rest days are important on a long trip, especially in harsh winter conditions. Use this day to do laundry, recharge devices, review photos, and plan the remaining days. Check the aurora forecast and weather for the week ahead.

day_by_day.morning: Drive the scenic Tröllaskagi peninsula — head south from Siglufjörður along Route 76 toward Hofsós. The drive through the mountains and along the coast is spectacular in winter. Stop at viewpoints along the way to photograph the fjords and snow-covered peaks.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit Hofsós, a tiny village on the east side of the Skagafjörður fjord. It is home to the Icelandic Emigration Centre (Vesturfarasetrið) which tells the story of Icelanders who emigrated to North America — entry around 1,500 ISK. The village also has a famous infinity-edge swimming pool overlooking the fjord (check winter opening hours).
day_by_day.evening: Drive back to Siglufjörður via Sauðárkrókur — the largest town in Skagafjörður with a population of about 2,600. Stop for supplies at the local supermarket before returning north. Watch for Northern Lights on the evening drive back through the mountains.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered early breakfast before the drive.
meals.lunch: Packed lunch eaten at a scenic viewpoint on the Tröllaskagi peninsula.
meals.dinner: Café in Sauðárkrókur — Kaffi Krókur or similar local café for a budget meal of soup and bread. Budget 1,800–2,500 ISK, or pick up groceries and cook at the hotel.

day_by_day.notes: The Hofsós swimming pool is one of Iceland's most scenic but may have limited winter hours — check ahead. The mountain roads on the Tröllaskagi peninsula can be challenging in winter — always check road.is. The total driving distance for this day trip is approximately 180km.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Varmahlíð in Skagafjörður valley, about 1 hour from Siglufjörður. Visit the Glaumbær turf farm museum — one of Iceland's best-preserved historic turf farmhouses, offering a fascinating glimpse into traditional Icelandic rural life. Entry around 2,000 ISK. The turf buildings date back to the 18th century.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Skagafjörður area — this region is famous for Icelandic horse breeding. Even in January you may spot herds of Icelandic horses in the fields. Drive along the valley and stop at the Víðimýrarkirkja turf church near Varmahlíð — one of Iceland's last remaining turf churches, free to view from outside.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Siglufjörður via the mountain road. Stop at the Reykir geothermal area near Varmahlíð if time allows — there is a small public hot pot (free or very low cost) that locals use. Arrive back in Siglufjörður for a quiet evening and Northern Lights watch.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered at the hotel.
meals.lunch: Café Aðalból at Glaumbær museum serves traditional Icelandic pancakes (pönnukökur) with cream and jam — a delicious and affordable treat at around 1,200–1,500 ISK.
meals.dinner: Self-catered dinner at the hotel — use up remaining grocery supplies for a simple but satisfying meal.

day_by_day.notes: Glaumbær museum may have reduced winter hours — confirm before visiting. The Skagafjörður valley is one of Iceland's most historically rich areas and is well worth exploring. Icelandic horses are a unique breed and cannot be exported — seeing them in their natural winter environment is a special experience.

day_by_day.morning: Dedicated Northern Lights morning — if there was a strong aurora display overnight, wake up early to catch any lingering activity. Otherwise, take a morning snowshoe walk or hike in the hills above Siglufjörður if conditions allow. The town is surrounded by excellent hiking terrain that transforms into a winter wonderland in January.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Siglufjörður Folk Music Centre (Þjóðlagasetur) if open — it celebrates Icelandic folk music traditions. Alternatively, spend the afternoon at the hotel reading, planning, or exploring the town's small art galleries and craft shops. Visit the local swimming pool (Sundlaug Siglufjarðar) for a warm soak — entry around 900–1,100 ISK.
day_by_day.evening: Aurora photography evening — if you have a smartphone with a night mode or a camera, set up on the harbour front or hillside for Northern Lights photography. The reflections of the aurora in the fjord waters can be spectacular. Bring hot drinks and dress in maximum layers.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered — a warm porridge (hafragrautur) with skyr and berries is a traditional Icelandic winter breakfast.
meals.lunch: Kaffi Rauðka for a warming lunch — fish and chips or lamb soup. Budget 2,000–2,500 ISK.
meals.dinner: Self-catered — try making skyr cake (skyr kaka) for dessert using local skyr, a fun and budget-friendly Icelandic cooking experience.

day_by_day.notes: The local swimming pool is an essential Icelandic social institution — even small towns like Siglufjörður have excellent geothermally heated pools. This is where locals gather and it is a wonderful cultural experience as well as a great way to warm up. January aurora activity can be very high — check KP index forecasts.

day_by_day.morning: Drive to Akureyri for a second visit — this time focus on the Botanical Garden (Lystigarðurinn), which is free to enter. While most plants are dormant in January, the garden's layout and the views over the fjord are still beautiful. Also visit the Nonni House (Nonnahús) — childhood home of author Jón Sveinsson, entry around 1,000 ISK.
day_by_day.afternoon: Explore the Akureyri Christmas Garden (Jólahúsið) — Iceland's famous Christmas shop that is open year-round and free to browse. Walk along the waterfront and visit the Akureyri Museum (Minjasafnið á Akureyri) for local history — entry around 1,500 ISK. Stock up on Bonus supermarket supplies for the final days.
day_by_day.evening: Visit the Akureyri Swimming Pool again for a relaxing soak in the outdoor hot pots before the drive back. Alternatively, if the Northern Lights forecast is strong, drive to a dark spot outside Akureyri — the area around Eyjafjörður offers excellent aurora viewing with the fjord as a foreground.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered early breakfast before departure.
meals.lunch: Bonus supermarket picnic in Akureyri — fresh bread, cheese, smoked lamb (hangikjöt), and skyr. Very budget-friendly at around 1,000–1,500 ISK total.
meals.dinner: Brynja ice cream shop is an Akureyri institution — treat yourself to Iceland's famous ice cream even in winter (Icelanders eat ice cream year-round!). For a proper dinner, Strikið offers good value or cook at the hotel on return.

day_by_day.notes: Use this Akureyri visit to stock up on all remaining grocery needs from Bonus — it will be significantly cheaper than the Samkaup-Strax in Siglufjörður. Pick up any souvenirs from the Christmas Garden or local craft shops as prices are generally lower than in Reykjavik.

day_by_day.morning: Explore the area around Siglufjörður that you haven't yet visited. Drive north along the fjord road as far as it goes — the road ends at the old avalanche barriers above town, offering dramatic views. Learn about Siglufjörður's history with avalanches — the town has been hit several times and the protective barriers are an engineering feat.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Siglufjörður swimming pool for a long, relaxing afternoon soak. The outdoor hot pots are perfect for a cold January afternoon. Alternatively, if there has been fresh snowfall, explore the snowy landscape around town on foot — the scenery is magical with fresh snow on the mountains.
day_by_day.evening: Final dedicated Northern Lights hunt of the trip. Drive to the darkest accessible spot near Siglufjörður — ideally along the fjord road away from town. Set up for a long aurora watch. January 2027 falls during a period of high solar activity (Solar Cycle 25 peak), making aurora sightings very likely on clear nights.

meals.breakfast: Self-catered — use up remaining breakfast supplies.
meals.lunch: Kaffi Rauðka for a farewell lunch in Siglufjörður — try the catch of the day for an authentic local experience. Budget 2,500–3,000 ISK.
meals.dinner: Special self-catered dinner at the hotel — cook a traditional Icelandic lamb stew (kjötsúpa) using lamb, root vegetables, and herbs. A fitting final dinner in Iceland.

day_by_day.notes: This is likely your last full evening in Siglufjörður — make the most of the Northern Lights opportunity. The KP index forecast from en.vedur.is is your best tool for planning the evening. Even a KP2-3 can produce visible aurora at this latitude (66°N — above the Arctic Circle).

day_by_day.morning: Final morning in Siglufjörður — take a last walk around the harbour and town. Visit any spots you missed during the trip. Take photographs of the town in the morning light. Check out of Hotel Siglunes and pack the car. Say goodbye to this remarkable little Arctic town.
day_by_day.afternoon: Begin the drive south toward Reykjavik (approximately 4.5–5 hours). Stop at Blönduós on Route 1 for a break and fuel. Continue through the Holtavörðuheiði highland plateau — a dramatic and desolate winter landscape. Stop at Hraunfossar and Barnafoss waterfalls near Borgarnes if time allows — free to visit and spectacular.
day_by_day.evening: Arrive in Reykjavik in the early evening. Check into a budget hostel or guesthouse — options like Kex Hostel, Loft Hostel, or Reykjavik Downtown Hostel offer dorm beds from 4,000–6,000 ISK or private rooms from 12,000–18,000 ISK. Explore the Laugavegur street area and the old harbour.

meals.breakfast: Final self-catered breakfast at the hotel in Siglufjörður — use up all remaining food supplies.
meals.lunch: Petrol station stop in Blönduós — hot dog and coffee, the classic Icelandic road trip meal at around 800–1,000 ISK.
meals.dinner: Reykjavik has many budget options — Hlöllabátar (Icelandic submarine sandwiches) on Laugavegur is excellent value at around 1,500–2,000 ISK, or try Noodle Station for warming Asian noodle soup at around 1,800 ISK.

day_by_day.notes: The drive from Siglufjörður to Reykjavik in January requires careful planning — check road.is thoroughly before departure. The highland sections of Route 1 can be icy. Allow extra time and do not rush. Book Reykjavik accommodation well in advance as January can still be busy with tourists.

day_by_day.morning: Final morning in Reykjavik — visit Hallgrímskirkja church (free to view outside, tower entry around 1,000 ISK for panoramic city views). Walk down Skólavörðustígur street to Laugavegur. Visit the Harpa Concert Hall on the harbour — free to enter the lobby and admire the stunning geometric glass architecture.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Settlement Exhibition (Landnámssýningin) — an underground museum built around a Viking Age longhouse discovered beneath Reykjavik, entry around 2,200 ISK. Alternatively, the National Museum of Iceland (Þjóðminjasafn Íslands) offers excellent coverage of Icelandic history for around 2,500 ISK. Head to Keflavik Airport in the afternoon — allow 45–60 minutes for the drive plus 2–3 hours for check-in.
day_by_day.evening: Depart from Keflavik International Airport. Reflect on 13 incredible days in Iceland — Northern Lights, geothermal hot springs, dramatic winter landscapes, and the unique culture of one of the world's most remote and remarkable countries.

meals.breakfast: Reykjavik Roasters or Te & Kaffi for a budget coffee and pastry — around 1,200–1,500 ISK. A treat for the final morning.
meals.lunch: Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur — Reykjavik's most famous hot dog stand near the harbour, a must-do Icelandic experience at around 600–700 ISK per hot dog.
meals.dinner: Airport meal or pack snacks for the flight — airport food is expensive so bring supplies from the city if possible.

day_by_day.notes: Return the rental car at Keflavik Airport — allow extra time for the return process. Do a final check of the accommodation and car for any left belongings. The Flybus from Reykjavik BSI to the airport runs regularly and costs around 3,500 ISK — book in advance online for the best price. Duty-free alcohol at Keflavik is significantly cheaper than in Reykjavik shops.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Keflavik International Airport at 06:10. Clear customs, collect luggage, and pick up pre-booked rental car (4WD essential for winter Iceland). Grab a coffee and light breakfast at the airport café before beginning the long drive north to Siglufjörður (approx. 5–6 hours via Route 1 and Tunnel). Drive through the Hvalfjörður tunnel and along the Snæfellsnes peninsula coastline for scenic winter views.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue driving north through Borgarnes and Varmahlíð. Stop at a roadside petrol station in Blönduós for a warm meal and fuel. Admire the dramatic winter landscape of the Skagafjörður valley as you approach the north. Arrive in Siglufjörður via the Héðinsfjörður tunnels in the late afternoon. Check in to Hotel Siglunes on Lækjargata 10 and settle into your room.
day_by_day.evening: Rest and recover from travel. Take a short stroll along the Siglufjörður harbour waterfront to get your bearings — the town is tiny and charming. Watch for the northern lights from the hotel or harbour area as Siglufjörður has very low light pollution. Early dinner at the hotel or a nearby local spot, then an early night to recover from the overnight flight.

meals.breakfast: Airport café at Keflavik — grab a skyr yoghurt, pastry, and coffee (~1,500 ISK)
meals.lunch: Roadside stop in Blönduós — petrol station grill or Kaffi Blönduós for soup and sandwich (~2,000 ISK)
meals.dinner: Sigló Hótel Restaurant or Hannes Boy restaurant in Siglufjörður — fresh fish soup and lamb (~4,500–6,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Drive carefully — January roads in northern Iceland can be icy and dark. Check road conditions at road.is before departing. Sunrise is very late (around 11:00) and sunset early (around 15:30) in January this far north. Pack snacks and water for the drive. Confirm hotel check-in time in advance as you may arrive before standard check-in.

day_by_day.morning: After a well-rested sleep, enjoy a hotel breakfast. Explore Siglufjörður on foot — visit the award-winning Herring Era Museum (Síldarminjasafnið), which tells the story of Iceland's herring boom in the early 20th century. The museum is one of Iceland's best regional museums and is open even in winter. Walk along the colourful harbour and admire the snow-capped mountains surrounding the fjord.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive the short scenic route through the Héðinsfjörður tunnel to neighbouring Ólafsfjörður (about 20 minutes). Explore this quiet fishing village and walk along its waterfront. Return to Siglufjörður and visit the local swimming pool (Sundlaug Siglufjarðar) — a classic Icelandic geothermal community pool with hot pots, perfect for warming up and meeting locals.
day_by_day.evening: Northern lights watch from the Siglufjörður harbour or the hillside above town. The fjord's remote location and minimal light pollution make it an excellent aurora-viewing spot. Bring warm layers, a thermos of hot chocolate, and a tripod if you have a camera. Check aurora forecast at en.vedur.is before heading out.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes breakfast buffet — included or ~2,000 ISK if not included; skyr, eggs, smoked salmon, rye bread
meals.lunch: Kaffi Rauðka in Siglufjörður — cosy café with homemade soups, sandwiches, and cakes (~2,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Hannes Boy restaurant — local favourite for fish and chips or lamb stew with Icelandic bread (~4,000–5,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: The Herring Era Museum may have limited winter hours — call ahead or check online. The community pool is a must-do Icelandic cultural experience and costs around 1,000 ISK. Aurora activity depends on cloud cover and solar activity; January offers long dark nights which maximise viewing windows.

day_by_day.morning: Drive south from Siglufjörður along Route 76 to Sauðárkrókur (about 1 hour), the largest town in the Skagafjörður region. Visit the Skagafjörður Heritage Museum (Byggðasafn Skagfirðinga) to learn about the region's Viking and farming history. Explore the town's small shops and bakery.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to the Glaumbær turf farm museum (about 20 minutes from Sauðárkrókur) — one of Iceland's best-preserved historic turf farmsteads, dating back to the 18th century. Walk through the low-ceilinged turf rooms and imagine life in medieval Iceland. Afterwards, visit the nearby Víðimýrarkirkja, a beautifully preserved 19th-century turf church. Return to Siglufjörður via the scenic Skagafjörður valley.
day_by_day.evening: Relax at the hotel. If skies are clear, head to the hillside above Siglufjörður for northern lights viewing — the mountains create a natural amphitheatre that frames the aurora beautifully. Alternatively, enjoy a quiet evening at the hotel with a book and a glass of Icelandic craft beer.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes — skyr with berries, rye bread with smoked lamb, coffee
meals.lunch: Café at Glaumbær (Áshús café) — traditional Icelandic pancakes with cream and jam, coffee (~1,800 ISK)
meals.dinner: Sigló Hótel Restaurant — pan-fried Arctic char with root vegetables and herb butter (~5,000–6,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Glaumbær is open in winter but with reduced hours (typically 10:00–16:00). Admission is around 2,000 ISK. The drive between Siglufjörður and Sauðárkrókur is scenic but can be icy — drive slowly and check road.is. Turf church visits are free.

day_by_day.morning: Drive east from Siglufjörður along the northern coast toward Akureyri, Iceland's second-largest city (about 1.5 hours via Route 82 and Route 1). Arrive in Akureyri and visit the iconic Akureyrarkirkja church perched on a hill above the town. Stroll down Hafnarstræti, the main pedestrian street, and browse local shops and galleries.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Akureyri Museum (Minjasafnið á Akureyri) for regional history and culture. Then head to the Akureyri Botanical Garden (Lystigarðurinn) — the world's northernmost botanical garden, beautiful even in winter with snow-covered sculptures and evergreen plantings. Soak in the Akureyri Swimming Pool (Sundlaug Akureyrar), which has excellent hot pots and a waterslide — a beloved local institution.
day_by_day.evening: Explore Akureyri's small but lively dining scene for dinner. If skies are clear, drive a few kilometres outside the city to escape light pollution for northern lights viewing. Return to Siglufjörður in the evening (1.5-hour drive — check road conditions carefully for night driving).

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes before departing — full Icelandic breakfast
meals.lunch: Bautinn Restaurant in Akureyri — classic Icelandic lamb soup and fresh bread, a local institution (~2,500–3,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Strikið Restaurant in Akureyri — mid-range Nordic cuisine with panoramic views of the fjord; try the lamb fillet (~5,500–7,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Akureyri is a full day trip from Siglufjörður. Consider whether to stay overnight in Akureyri to avoid the late-night drive back — budget guesthouses are available for ~12,000–15,000 ISK. The swimming pool costs around 1,000 ISK. Akureyri has good supermarkets (Krónan, Nettó) — stock up on snacks and supplies.

day_by_day.morning: Rest morning in Siglufjörður. Sleep in and enjoy a leisurely hotel breakfast. Walk along the harbour in the late morning light (sunrise around 11:00) and photograph the colourful fishing boats against the snow-covered mountains. Visit the small local grocery store to pick up supplies.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to the Secret Lagoon Natural Hot Spring (Gamla Laugin) in Flúðir — this is a longer drive of about 3.5–4 hours south via Route 1. The Secret Lagoon is Iceland's oldest swimming pool, a naturally heated geothermal pool at around 38–40°C, surrounded by bubbling hot springs and geysers. Soak and relax in the steaming waters surrounded by a snowy winter landscape — a magical experience.
day_by_day.evening: Stay overnight in the Flúðir/South Iceland area to avoid the long drive back north. Book a guesthouse or farmstay in the area (e.g., Guesthouse Flúðir or nearby farmstay, ~12,000–16,000 ISK). Enjoy a quiet dinner in the village and watch for northern lights over the open south Iceland plains.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes — leisurely breakfast with skyr, eggs, and coffee
meals.lunch: Pack a picnic lunch from the hotel or local shop — rye bread, smoked salmon, cheese, and fruit for the road
meals.dinner: Guesthouse Flúðir restaurant or Lindin Restaurant in Laugarvatn (30 min away) — geothermal-cooked food, lamb and fish (~4,500–6,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Secret Lagoon admission is approximately 3,500 ISK. Book in advance online as it can sell out even in winter. Bring a swimsuit, towel (or rent one for ~700 ISK), and waterproof bag for your belongings. The drive south is long — depart by noon to arrive with daylight. This overnight away from Siglufjörður allows exploration of South Iceland over the next two days.

day_by_day.morning: Drive east along the Golden Circle route. Visit Þingvellir National Park (Thingvellir) — a UNESCO World Heritage Site where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates meet and where Iceland's first parliament was established in 930 AD. Walk along the Almannagjá rift valley and admire the dramatic geology. The park is stunning in winter with frost and snow.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue to the Geysir Geothermal Area to watch Strokkur geyser erupt every 5–10 minutes, shooting boiling water 20–30 metres into the air. Then visit the powerful Gullfoss waterfall — partially frozen in January, creating spectacular ice formations around the cascading water. These are two of Iceland's most iconic natural sights.
day_by_day.evening: Drive to Reykjavik (about 1.5 hours from Gullfoss) and check in to a mid-range guesthouse or hotel for one night (e.g., Guesthouse Butterfly or similar, ~15,000–20,000 ISK). Explore Reykjavik's Laugavegur street in the evening and enjoy dinner in the capital.

meals.breakfast: Guesthouse in Flúðir — included breakfast or local café
meals.lunch: Geysir Centre café — lamb soup and Icelandic bread at the visitor centre (~2,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Reykjavik — Sægreifinn (The Sea Baron) on the old harbour — famous lobster soup and grilled fish skewers (~3,500–4,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Þingvellir, Geysir, and Gullfoss form the classic Golden Circle — all within a few hours of each other. Þingvellir National Park is free to enter (parking fee ~750 ISK). Dress in full waterproof layers at Gullfoss as spray from the falls can drench you even in winter. Roads may be icy — drive carefully.

day_by_day.morning: Blue Lagoon Geothermal Spa experience — drive from Reykjavik to the Blue Lagoon on the Reykjanes Peninsula (about 45 minutes). Soak in the world-famous milky-blue geothermal waters rich in silica and minerals. Enjoy the in-water bar, silica mud mask, and the surreal experience of bathing in 37–39°C water surrounded by black lava fields. Book the Comfort package for a mid-range experience including towel and silica mask.
day_by_day.afternoon: After the Blue Lagoon, drive back toward Reykjavik. Explore the city properly — visit Hallgrímskirkja church (take the lift to the top for panoramic views, ~1,000 ISK), walk through the old town, and visit the Harpa Concert Hall on the waterfront. Browse the shops on Laugavegur for Icelandic wool sweaters (lopapeysa) and local design.
day_by_day.evening: Northern Lights Hunting Tour from Reykjavik — join a guided evening minibus tour that drives away from the city's light pollution to find the best aurora viewing spots based on that night's forecast. Tours typically run 21:00–00:00 and include expert guides with photography tips. This is one of the listed key experiences.

meals.breakfast: Reykjavik guesthouse — included breakfast or Brauð & Co bakery on Frakkastígur for fresh sourdough and coffee (~1,500 ISK)
meals.lunch: Reykjavik — Messinn restaurant — pan-fried fish of the day in cast iron skillet, a local favourite (~3,500–4,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Pre-tour light dinner — Noodle Station on Laugavegur for warming ramen-style soup (~2,000 ISK) before the northern lights tour

day_by_day.notes: Blue Lagoon Comfort package costs approximately 14,990 ISK — book well in advance as it sells out months ahead. Northern Lights tour costs approximately 8,000–10,000 ISK per person — book through Reykjavik Excursions or Arctic Adventures. Tours are weather-dependent and reputable operators offer free rebooking if conditions are poor. Check out of Reykjavik accommodation and store luggage at the hotel if needed.

day_by_day.morning: Drive east from Reykjavik along the South Coast (Route 1). Stop at Seljalandsfoss waterfall — in January it may be partially frozen, creating stunning ice curtains. You can walk behind the falls in summer but in winter enjoy it from the front. Continue to Skógafoss waterfall, another dramatic cascade with a rainbow on sunny days and ice formations in winter.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue east to Vík í Mýrdal — Iceland's southernmost village. Walk to the black sand beach of Reynisfjara (with extreme caution — sneaker waves are deadly year-round). Admire the basalt column sea stacks (Reynisdrangar) rising from the ocean. Visit the Reyniskirkja church on the hill above Vík for panoramic coastal views. Check in to accommodation in or near Vík (e.g., Hótel Vík í Mýrdal or guesthouse, ~15,000–20,000 ISK).
day_by_day.evening: Northern lights watch from the open black sand beach or hillside above Vík — the South Coast has wide open skies with minimal light pollution. The contrast of the aurora over the dark ocean and black beach is extraordinary. Enjoy a warm dinner in Vík before heading out.

meals.breakfast: Reykjavik — grab coffee and pastry from a bakery before departing early
meals.lunch: Skógarfoss area — Skógafoss Café or packed lunch from Reykjavik supermarket (~2,000 ISK)
meals.dinner: Suður-Vík Restaurant in Vík — fish and chips, lamb burger, or fish stew with local bread (~4,000–5,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: NEVER turn your back on the ocean at Reynisfjara — sneaker waves have killed visitors. Stay well back from the waterline. Seljalandsfoss path behind the falls is closed in winter due to ice. The South Coast drive is one of Iceland's most scenic — allow extra time for stops and photography. Check road.is for conditions on Route 1.

day_by_day.morning: Drive east from Vík toward Skaftafell in Vatnajökull National Park (about 1.5 hours). Stop at the Eldhraun lava field — a vast moss-covered lava plain from the 1783 Laki eruption, eerily beautiful in winter. Also stop at Fjaðrárgljúfur canyon if road conditions allow — a dramatic 100-metre-deep canyon carved by glacial floods.
day_by_day.afternoon: Skaftafell Glacier Hike on Vatnajökull — join a guided glacier hike on Europe's largest glacier. Strap on crampons and an ice axe and walk across the blue ice with an expert guide. Explore stunning ice formations, crevasses, and moulins. The hike typically lasts 2–3 hours and is suitable for beginners. This is one of the listed key experiences and is unforgettable in winter when the ice is at its most dramatic.
day_by_day.evening: Drive to the Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon (about 45 minutes east of Skaftafell). In the fading light or darkness, watch icebergs calving from the Breiðamerkurjökull glacier and floating in the lagoon. The nearby Diamond Beach has ice chunks washed up on black sand — magical in any light. Return to accommodation near Skaftafell or Höfn (~15,000–18,000 ISK).

meals.breakfast: Hótel Vík or guesthouse — full Icelandic breakfast before the drive
meals.lunch: Skaftafell Visitor Centre café — soup and sandwich before the glacier hike (~2,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Jökulsárlón area — Glacier Goose café (if open) or drive to Höfn for dinner at Humarhöfnin (Lobster House) — famous for Icelandic langoustine (~5,500–7,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Glacier hike must be booked in advance through Icelandic Mountain Guides or similar operator (~12,000–15,000 ISK). Wear warm, waterproof layers — the glacier is extremely cold and windy. All equipment (crampons, helmet, harness) is provided. Jökulsárlón is free to visit. Höfn is known as the langoustine capital of Iceland — dinner there is a must if you enjoy seafood.

day_by_day.morning: Return to Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon at dawn (around 11:00) for the best light on the icebergs. Take a slow walk along Diamond Beach collecting photographs of ice sculptures on the black sand. Drive west back along the South Coast, stopping at the Foss á Síðu waterfall and the turf church at Núpsstaður.
day_by_day.afternoon: Snorkeling or Diving in Silfra Fissure — drive to Þingvellir National Park (about 3.5 hours from the Skaftafell area). Join an afternoon guided snorkelling tour in Silfra, where you float between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates in crystal-clear glacial water with visibility over 100 metres. The water is 2–4°C but dry suits keep you warm. This is one of the listed key experiences and one of the world's top dive sites.
day_by_day.evening: Drive to Reykjavik or the Þingvellir area for overnight accommodation. Warm up with a hot shower and a hearty dinner. Celebrate the incredible experiences of the past few days.

meals.breakfast: Höfn guesthouse — included breakfast or local bakery
meals.lunch: Packed lunch or roadside stop — thermos of soup and sandwiches for the long drive
meals.dinner: Reykjavik or Þingvellir area — Friðheimar tomato farm restaurant (book ahead) — unique greenhouse dining with tomato-based menu (~4,500–6,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Silfra snorkelling must be booked well in advance through Dive.is or Arctic Adventures (~19,000–22,000 ISK including dry suit). You must be a confident swimmer. The water is extremely cold — follow all guide instructions. This is a long driving day — consider splitting the drive with an overnight stop near Vík. Friðheimar restaurant requires advance booking.

day_by_day.morning: Begin the long drive back north to Siglufjörður (approximately 5–6 hours). Drive through the Hvalfjörður tunnel and north along Route 1 through Borgarnes. Stop at the Settlement Centre in Borgarnes (Landnámssetur) — an excellent museum about Iceland's Viking settlement and the Egils Saga, one of Iceland's greatest medieval sagas (~2,000 ISK admission).
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue north through Varmahlíð and Sauðárkrókur. Stop at the Hofsós swimming pool — a stunning infinity-edge geothermal pool overlooking the Skagafjörður fjord, considered one of Iceland's most beautiful community pools. Soak in the hot pots with views of the fjord and distant mountains (~1,000 ISK).
day_by_day.evening: Arrive back in Siglufjörður in the early evening. Enjoy a welcome return to Hotel Siglunes. Take a quiet walk along the familiar harbour and watch for northern lights over the fjord. Enjoy a relaxed dinner at your favourite local restaurant.

meals.breakfast: Reykjavik or Þingvellir accommodation — full breakfast before the long drive
meals.lunch: Settlement Centre café in Borgarnes — lamb soup and Icelandic bread (~2,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Hannes Boy restaurant in Siglufjörður — welcome back with fresh fish of the day and local beer (~4,500–5,500 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: The Hofsós pool is one of Iceland's hidden gems — worth the short detour off Route 1. It may have limited winter hours, so check ahead. The drive back to Siglufjörður through the Héðinsfjörður tunnels can be icy at night — take care. It's good to be back in your home base for the final days of the trip.

day_by_day.morning: Leisurely morning in Siglufjörður. Sleep in and enjoy a slow breakfast. Visit the Herring Era Museum again if you want to explore exhibits you missed on Day 2. Walk up the hillside above town for panoramic views of the fjord and surrounding mountains — on a clear day the views are extraordinary.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive to Dalvík (about 45 minutes from Siglufjörður via the Ólafsfjörður tunnel). Visit the Hvoll Museum in Dalvík — a quirky local museum with exhibits on the 1934 earthquake and a famous giant Icelander. Then take the ferry or drive to explore the Tröllaskagi (Troll Peninsula) mountain roads if conditions allow — some of the most dramatic mountain scenery in Iceland. Return to Siglufjörður via the scenic coastal route.
day_by_day.evening: Final dedicated northern lights evening. Drive to the hillside above Siglufjörður or along the fjord road away from town for the best aurora viewing. Bring a thermos of hot chocolate, warm blankets, and your camera. Spend 1–2 hours watching and photographing the aurora borealis dancing over the snow-covered mountains and fjord — a perfect final night memory.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes — leisurely full breakfast with all the Icelandic classics
meals.lunch: Kaffi Rauðka in Siglufjörður — homemade cake, soup, and coffee in the cosy café (~2,000 ISK)
meals.dinner: Sigló Hótel Restaurant — splurge slightly on a special final dinner; try the lamb rack with root vegetable purée and Icelandic herbs (~6,000–8,000 ISK)

day_by_day.notes: Check the aurora forecast at en.vedur.is and the cloud cover map carefully for the best viewing window tonight. The Tröllaskagi mountain roads (Route 82) may be closed or require 4WD in January — check road.is before attempting. Dalvík is a charming small town worth a brief visit. Consider buying local Icelandic souvenirs in Siglufjörður today.

day_by_day.morning: Final morning in Siglufjörður. Pack and check out of Hotel Siglunes. Take one last walk along the harbour and say goodbye to this beautiful remote town. Begin the drive south toward Keflavik Airport (approximately 5.5–6 hours). Drive through the Skagafjörður valley and south along Route 1.
day_by_day.afternoon: Stop in Borgarnes for a final Icelandic lunch. Continue south toward Reykjavik and Keflavik. If time allows, make a brief stop at the Reykjanes Peninsula lava fields or the Bridge Between Continents (a small footbridge symbolically spanning the tectonic plates) near Keflavik. Return the rental car at Keflavik Airport and check in for your departure flight.
day_by_day.evening: Departure from Keflavik International Airport. Enjoy a final Icelandic hot dog (pylsur) from the airport kiosk — a beloved Icelandic tradition — before boarding. Reflect on 13 extraordinary days of northern lights, hot springs, glaciers, waterfalls, and the raw beauty of Iceland in winter.

meals.breakfast: Hotel Siglunes — final Icelandic breakfast; savour the skyr, smoked salmon, and rye bread one last time
meals.lunch: Borgarnes — Hyrnan restaurant or the Settlement Centre café — lamb soup and fresh bread for the road (~2,500 ISK)
meals.dinner: Keflavik Airport — airport restaurant or café for a final meal before departure; or pack snacks from a Reykjavik supermarket

day_by_day.notes: Allow at least 2.5–3 hours at Keflavik Airport before your flight for car return, check-in, and security. The car rental return is at the airport — factor in the shuttle bus time from the car park. Buy any last-minute Icelandic souvenirs (skyr, Brennivín schnapps, lopapeysa wool items) at the airport duty-free. Check your flight departure time carefully and plan the drive accordingly — do not rush on icy winter roads.

highlights: Mix of paid and free experiences

trip_options.title: Premium Iceland Escape
trip_options.description: Indulge in the best the destination has to offer. Premium flights, luxury hotels, and exclusive experiences.

experiences.name: Northern Lights Hunting Tour
experiences.description: Join a guided evening tour away from Reykjavik's light pollution to witness the aurora borealis dancing across the sky. Expert guides use real-time forecasts to find the best viewing spots, and you'll learn about the science behind this natural phenomenon while capturing stunning photographs.

experiences.name: Blue Lagoon Geothermal Spa
experiences.description: Soak in the world-famous milky-blue geothermal waters rich in silica and minerals. Enjoy in-water massages, silica mud masks, and swim-up bars while surrounded by dramatic lava fields. Book the Comfort package for access to the main lagoon, towel rental, and one silica mud mask.

experiences.name: Snorkeling or Diving in Silfra Fissure
experiences.description: Snorkel or dive between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates in crystal-clear glacial water with visibility up to 100 meters. The surreal blue and green hues of the water make this one of the most unique natural experiences on Earth, guided by certified instructors.

experiences.name: Secret Lagoon Natural Hot Spring
experiences.description: Relax in Iceland's oldest swimming pool, a naturally heated geothermal pool surrounded by bubbling hot springs and a small geyser that erupts every few minutes. Far less crowded than the Blue Lagoon, this authentic experience offers a peaceful soak amid stunning Icelandic countryside.

experiences.name: Skaftafell Glacier Hike on Vatnajökull
experiences.description: Strap on crampons and hike across Europe's largest glacier with an expert guide. Explore stunning ice formations, deep blue crevasses, and ash layers from ancient volcanic eruptions. The hike offers breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding black sand plains and mountain peaks.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Keflavík International Airport at 06:10. Clear customs and collect luggage. Transfer via private luxury vehicle (pre-arranged chauffeur service) toward Reykjavik for a brief orientation stop before beginning the long scenic drive north to Siglufjörður. The drive (~5–6 hours) winds through dramatic lava fields, snow-dusted mountains, and coastal fjords — a breathtaking introduction to Iceland in winter.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue the scenic drive north along Route 1 and then Route 76 into the Tröllaskagi Peninsula. Stop at Hofsós Infinity Pool — a geothermal swimming pool perched dramatically above Skagafjörður fjord — for a warm, restorative soak after the long flight. Arrive at Hotel Siglunes in Siglufjörður by late afternoon. Check in, unpack, and settle into your premium room overlooking the fjord.
day_by_day.evening: Rest and recover from travel. Step outside briefly to scan the sky for the northern lights — Siglufjörður's remote location and minimal light pollution make it an exceptional aurora-viewing spot. Bundle up and walk along the quiet harbor front for a first taste of this charming fishing village.

meals.breakfast: Light refreshments at Keflavík Airport's premium lounge (Saga Lounge) before or after landing — grab a coffee and pastry to start the day.
meals.lunch: Stop en route at Gauksmýri Lodge Restaurant near Hvammstangi — a cozy, upscale farm-to-table spot serving hearty Icelandic lamb soup and fresh bread, perfect for a mid-journey warm-up.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Hannes Boy Restaurant in Siglufjörður — the town's finest dining establishment, celebrated for its fresh Arctic char, locally caught cod, and Icelandic lamb, served in a warm, intimate atmosphere.

day_by_day.notes: Dress in thermal layers for the drive and outdoor stops. January days are very short in northern Iceland (roughly 5–6 hours of daylight), so the drive will be partly in darkness — the chauffeur will be experienced with winter road conditions. Pre-book the Hofsós Pool stop in advance. Aurora forecast apps (e.g., Vedur.is) are recommended to track activity each evening.

day_by_day.morning: After a leisurely breakfast at the hotel, embark on a guided snowshoe or winter hiking tour in the mountains directly above Siglufjörður. The town is nestled between dramatic peaks that offer stunning views of the fjord below. A local guide will lead you through snow-covered trails, pointing out Arctic wildlife tracks and geological features unique to this remote peninsula.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the award-winning Herring Era Museum (Síldarminjasafnið) — one of Iceland's finest regional museums, spread across three renovated harbor buildings. Explore the fascinating history of the 20th-century herring boom that made Siglufjörður the 'herring capital of the world.' Afterward, warm up with a private geothermal pool session — Hotel Siglunes can arrange access to local hot pots for guests.
day_by_day.evening: Northern Lights hunting from the hillsides above Siglufjörður. The town's position deep in a fjord, surrounded by mountains, creates a natural amphitheater with dark skies ideal for aurora viewing. Bring a thermos of hot cocoa, a tripod for photography, and warm blankets. If clouds obscure the view, enjoy a cozy evening in the hotel lounge with Icelandic schnapps (brennivín).

meals.breakfast: Full Icelandic breakfast at Hotel Siglunes — skyr with berries, smoked salmon on rye bread (rúgbrauð), soft-boiled eggs, Icelandic butter, and strong coffee.
meals.lunch: Café Rauðka in Siglufjörður — a charming local café serving homemade soups, open-faced sandwiches, and freshly baked cinnamon rolls (snúður). A beloved local institution.
meals.dinner: Return to Hannes Boy or request a private in-hotel dining experience — ask the hotel to arrange a chef's tasting menu featuring seasonal Icelandic ingredients such as reindeer, langoustine, and Arctic herbs.

day_by_day.notes: January in Siglufjörður can bring heavy snowfall and strong winds — always check local weather and road conditions before outdoor excursions. The Herring Era Museum may have limited winter hours; confirm in advance. Aurora activity peaks between 10 PM and 2 AM — plan evening activities accordingly.

day_by_day.morning: Take a private guided ice fishing excursion on one of the frozen lakes near Siglufjörður or in the Tröllaskagi highlands. A local expert will drill holes in the ice and teach you traditional Icelandic ice fishing techniques. This serene, meditative winter activity offers a deeply authentic Arctic experience surrounded by snow-blanketed mountains.
day_by_day.afternoon: Drive the scenic Héðinsfjörður tunnel route to explore the abandoned village of Héðinsfjörður — a hauntingly beautiful ghost settlement evacuated in 1951, now accessible via a mountain tunnel. Walk among the ruins of old farmhouses buried in snow, with dramatic fjord views all around. Return to Siglufjörður for a warm geothermal hot tub session at the local swimming pool (Sundlaug Siglufjarðar).
day_by_day.evening: Aurora watching from a private vantage point arranged by the hotel — a guided 2-hour evening excursion to a dark-sky location above the fjord, with a local aurora expert who will explain the science and mythology of the northern lights. Hot drinks and warm blankets provided.

meals.breakfast: Skyr parfait with Icelandic granola and wild crowberries, fresh pastries, and coffee at Hotel Siglunes.
meals.lunch: Packed gourmet lunch prepared by the hotel for the ice fishing excursion — smoked lamb sandwiches, thermos of lamb soup, Icelandic chocolate, and hot coffee.
meals.dinner: Private dinner at Hotel Siglunes featuring a curated three-course menu: langoustine bisque, pan-seared Arctic char with dill butter and root vegetables, and skyr panna cotta with crowberry compote.

day_by_day.notes: Ice fishing requires warm, waterproof clothing and sturdy boots — the hotel can arrange rental gear if needed. The Héðinsfjörður tunnel is generally open in winter but check conditions. Aurora excursions should be booked through the hotel concierge who monitors nightly KP index forecasts.

day_by_day.morning: Depart Siglufjörður by private vehicle for a full-day excursion to the Snæfellsnes Peninsula (approximately 3.5–4 hours south). The drive itself is spectacular — crossing the Tröllaskagi Peninsula, passing through Akureyri (Iceland's 'Capital of the North'), and heading south along the western fjords. Stop in Akureyri for a brief morning walk along the main street and a visit to the iconic Akureyrarkirkja church.
day_by_day.afternoon: Arrive at Snæfellsnes Peninsula and explore Snæfellsjökull National Park — the mystical glacier-capped volcano immortalized in Jules Verne's 'Journey to the Center of the Earth.' Walk along the dramatic Djúpalónssandur black pebble beach, explore the Lóndrangar basalt sea stacks, and visit the eerie Vatnshellir lava tube cave with a guided tour. The landscape feels otherworldly in winter.
day_by_day.evening: Return drive toward Siglufjörður, stopping for dinner in Akureyri before continuing north. Arrive back at the hotel by late evening. Check aurora forecasts and step outside for a sky scan before retiring.

meals.breakfast: Early breakfast at Hotel Siglunes before departure — smoked salmon, eggs, and coffee.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Narfeyrarstofa Restaurant in Snæfellsnes — a beloved farmhouse restaurant serving traditional Icelandic lamb and fish dishes in a rustic, elegant setting.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Rub23 in Akureyri — one of Iceland's most acclaimed restaurants outside Reykjavik, renowned for its creative sushi and premium Icelandic meat and seafood dishes with Asian-Nordic fusion flair.

day_by_day.notes: This is a long driving day (~7–8 hours total) — a private driver is strongly recommended. January road conditions on Route 1 can be icy; ensure the vehicle has studded winter tires. The Vatnshellir cave tour must be pre-booked. Snæfellsnes is worth the journey for its extraordinary volcanic and coastal scenery.

day_by_day.morning: Rest and recovery morning at Hotel Siglunes. Enjoy a slow, indulgent breakfast and then take a leisurely walk through Siglufjörður's charming streets — admire the colorful wooden houses, the quiet harbor, and the dramatic mountain backdrop. Visit the small but excellent Folk Music Center (Þórbergssetur) if open, celebrating Iceland's rich tradition of folk song (rímur).
day_by_day.afternoon: Private whale watching and seabird boat tour from Siglufjörður harbor (winter tours operate with smaller, heated vessels). The waters around the Tröllaskagi Peninsula are rich in humpback whales, minke whales, white-beaked dolphins, and seabirds even in January. A marine biologist guide accompanies the tour. Alternatively, if sea conditions are rough, opt for a private photography workshop in the fjord landscape with a local professional photographer.
day_by_day.evening: Relaxed evening at the hotel. Enjoy the hotel's facilities, read by the fire, and monitor aurora forecasts. If KP index is favorable (≥3), venture out to the harbor or hillside for aurora photography. The hotel concierge can arrange a private aurora guide on short notice.

meals.breakfast: Leisurely full Icelandic breakfast at Hotel Siglunes — take your time with fresh pastries, skyr, smoked fish, and multiple coffees.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at Café Rauðka — homemade fish soup, fresh bread, and a slice of Icelandic layer cake (vínarterta).
meals.dinner: Dinner at Hannes Boy — order the chef's special catch of the day, paired with a curated Icelandic wine selection. Finish with a traditional Icelandic dessert and a glass of Brennivín.

day_by_day.notes: Whale watching in January is weather-dependent — confirm with the operator on the morning of the tour. Dress in full waterproof gear for the boat. The Folk Music Center may have limited winter hours. This is a good day to recharge before more active days ahead.

day_by_day.morning: Depart early for a full-day excursion to the Mývatn region (approximately 1.5 hours east of Siglufjörður via the mountain road or 2 hours via Route 1). Arrive at Lake Mývatn — one of Iceland's most geologically active and visually stunning areas. Begin with a walk around the extraordinary Dimmuborgir lava formations — a labyrinthine landscape of twisted lava pillars and arches, mythologically linked to trolls and the entrance to the underworld.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Námaskarð geothermal area (Hverir) — a surreal, steaming landscape of bubbling mud pools, sulfurous fumaroles, and vivid orange and yellow mineral deposits. Then soak in the Mývatn Nature Baths — often called the 'Blue Lagoon of the North,' these geothermal pools offer a more intimate, less crowded experience with stunning views of the volcanic landscape. Enjoy the premium facilities including private changing rooms and a geothermal steam bath.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Siglufjörður by early evening. The drive back through the highlands may offer spectacular aurora views if skies are clear — ask your driver to stop at a dark-sky pullout for photos. Arrive at the hotel for a late dinner.

meals.breakfast: Early packed breakfast from Hotel Siglunes — thermos of coffee, smoked lamb sandwiches, and Icelandic pastries for the road.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Vogafjós Farm Restaurant at Lake Mývatn — a unique farm-to-table experience where you can watch cows being milked through a glass window while dining on fresh geothermal rye bread, smoked trout, and homemade ice cream.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Gamli Bærinn (The Old Farmhouse) near Mývatn, or return to Siglufjörður for a late dinner at Hannes Boy — call ahead to arrange a late reservation.

day_by_day.notes: The mountain road (Route 82) between Siglufjörður and Mývatn may be closed in severe winter weather — always check road.is before departure. Mývatn Nature Baths should be pre-booked. Bring swimwear and a towel, or rent them on-site. The Hverir geothermal area is free to visit but can be slippery — wear sturdy boots.

day_by_day.morning: Embark on a private snowmobile tour in the mountains above Siglufjörður or in the Tröllaskagi highlands. A guided snowmobile excursion through pristine Arctic snowfields, with panoramic views of the fjords below, is one of the most exhilarating winter experiences in northern Iceland. No prior experience necessary — guides provide full instruction and safety briefing.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Siglufjörður and visit the Herring Era Museum more thoroughly if not fully explored on Day 2 — the museum's three buildings contain remarkable exhibits on the herring industry, complete with restored boats, processing equipment, and period costumes. Afterward, enjoy a private geothermal hot tub session arranged by the hotel, followed by a relaxing massage at the hotel spa (if available) or a nearby wellness center.
day_by_day.evening: Dedicated northern lights evening. The hotel concierge will have monitored the week's aurora forecasts and identified the best viewing night — tonight is reserved as the prime aurora hunting opportunity. A private guide with a 4WD vehicle will take you to the optimal dark-sky location above the fjord. Champagne and warm blankets provided. Professional aurora photography assistance available.

meals.breakfast: Full Icelandic breakfast at Hotel Siglunes — eggs your way, smoked salmon, skyr, fresh juice, and coffee.
meals.lunch: Warm lunch at the hotel after the snowmobile tour — hearty lamb stew (kjötsúpa), fresh bread, and hot chocolate.
meals.dinner: Special premium dinner at Hotel Siglunes — request a private dining setup with candles and a curated tasting menu: amuse-bouche, langoustine carpaccio, reindeer tenderloin with juniper berry sauce, artisan Icelandic cheeses, and a skyr-based dessert. Paired with Icelandic craft beers or imported wines.

day_by_day.notes: Snowmobile tours require a valid driver's license. Minimum age is typically 18 to drive; younger guests can ride as passengers. Dress in full thermal layers — the hotel can arrange snowmobile suits. The aurora private tour should be confirmed by 6 PM based on that evening's forecast. KP index of 3 or above with clear skies gives excellent viewing chances.

day_by_day.morning: Depart Siglufjörður for a multi-day excursion south. Drive to Akureyri (1 hour) and then fly or drive south toward Reykjavik. If driving, take the scenic Route 1 along the east coast of the Skagafjörður fjord, stopping at Glaumbær Turf Farm Museum — a beautifully preserved 18th-century turf farmhouse complex that offers a vivid glimpse into traditional Icelandic rural life. Continue south through the Holtavörðuheiði highland plateau.
day_by_day.afternoon: Arrive in the Reykjavik area by mid-afternoon. Check into a luxury Reykjavik hotel (e.g., The Retreat at Blue Lagoon, Hotel Borg, or ION Adventure Hotel) for a two-night stay. Freshen up and explore Reykjavik's compact but vibrant city center — walk along Laugavegur shopping street, visit Hallgrímskirkja church, and browse the design boutiques and galleries.
day_by_day.evening: Explore Reykjavik's legendary nightlife and dining scene. Visit the Harpa Concert Hall for an evening concert or simply admire its stunning geometric glass facade illuminated at night. Stroll the old harbor area.

meals.breakfast: Final breakfast at Hotel Siglunes before departure — savor the fjord views one last time over coffee and fresh pastries.
meals.lunch: Stop at Glaumbær café for traditional Icelandic pancakes (pönnukökur) with cream and jam — a classic Icelandic treat in a historic setting.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Dill Restaurant in Reykjavik — Iceland's first Michelin-starred restaurant, offering a stunning New Nordic tasting menu that celebrates Icelandic ingredients with extraordinary creativity. Pre-booking essential.

day_by_day.notes: If flying Akureyri to Reykjavik (Air Iceland Connect), book in advance — flights are short (45 min) and convenient. If driving, the Route 1 journey is approximately 5–6 hours. Confirm luxury Reykjavik hotel reservation well in advance, especially for The Retreat at Blue Lagoon which books out months ahead. Dill Restaurant requires advance reservation.

day_by_day.morning: Experience the world-famous Blue Lagoon Geothermal Spa — book the premium 'Retreat Spa' package for the ultimate luxury experience. Soak in the iconic milky-blue silica-rich geothermal waters, enjoy an in-water massage, apply silica mud masks, and relax in the exclusive Retreat Lagoon (reserved for Retreat Hotel guests or premium day visitors). The steam caves, sauna, and cold plunge pools complete the experience.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Reykjavik and explore the National Museum of Iceland (Þjóðminjasafn Íslands) for a deep dive into 1,200 years of Icelandic history and culture. Afterward, visit the Settlement Exhibition (Landnámssýningin) — built around an actual Viking-age longhouse excavated beneath the city streets. Browse the boutiques of Skólavörðustígur street for premium Icelandic wool goods, design items, and local art.
day_by_day.evening: Northern Lights Hunting Tour from Reykjavik — join a premium guided evening excursion by super-jeep to dark-sky locations outside the city. Expert guides monitor aurora forecasts in real time and drive to optimal viewing spots. Hot drinks and photography tips included. If aurora activity is low, the tour visits dramatic lava field landscapes illuminated under starlight.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at your Reykjavik luxury hotel — full buffet or à la carte with Icelandic specialties.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at the Blue Lagoon's premium Lava Restaurant — enjoy a meal overlooking the steaming lagoon, featuring Icelandic seafood and seasonal dishes.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Grillið Restaurant atop the Radisson Blu Saga Hotel — Reykjavik's most elegant rooftop dining experience with panoramic city views, serving premium Icelandic lamb, lobster, and seasonal tasting menus.

day_by_day.notes: Blue Lagoon Retreat Spa packages must be booked weeks or months in advance — this is non-negotiable for premium access. Bring a swimsuit (or purchase one on-site). The evening aurora tour departs around 9–10 PM; dress in maximum warmth. January offers the longest aurora-viewing windows of the year (darkness from ~4 PM to ~11 AM).

day_by_day.morning: Embark on the iconic Golden Circle tour by private luxury vehicle with a personal guide. Begin at Þingvellir National Park — a UNESCO World Heritage Site where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates meet and where Iceland's ancient parliament (Alþingi) was founded in 930 AD. Walk along the dramatic Almannagjá rift valley in a winter wonderland of snow and ice.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue the Golden Circle to the Geysir Geothermal Area — watch Strokkur geyser erupt every 5–10 minutes, shooting boiling water 20–40 meters into the frigid air. Then visit the majestic Gullfoss waterfall — partially frozen in January, creating an extraordinary spectacle of ice, mist, and thundering water. The winter light (golden hour lasts most of the short day) makes photography exceptional.
day_by_day.evening: Snorkeling or Diving in Silfra Fissure — experience one of the world's most unique dive sites, located within Þingvellir National Park. Drift through crystal-clear glacial water (visibility up to 100 meters) between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. Dry suits are provided for warmth. This is a bucket-list experience unlike anything else on Earth. Book the premium guided dive package.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at your Reykjavik hotel before departure.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Friðheimar Greenhouse Restaurant near Geysir — a unique dining experience inside a working tomato greenhouse, serving tomato-based dishes, fresh tomato soup, and Bloody Marys made from their own produce.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Matur og Drykkur in Reykjavik — a celebrated restaurant specializing in traditional Icelandic recipes reimagined with modern technique. Try the salt cod head, fermented shark, and other heritage dishes in an elegant setting.

day_by_day.notes: Silfra snorkeling/diving requires advance booking and a medical fitness declaration. Minimum water temperature is 2–4°C — dry suits keep you warm but the face will feel the cold. Non-swimmers can snorkel with a guide. The Golden Circle is approximately 300 km round trip from Reykjavik — a full day with a private guide is the most comfortable option.

day_by_day.morning: Depart Reykjavik early for the South Coast — one of Iceland's most dramatic and accessible regions. Drive along Route 1 past the Eyjafjallajökull volcano (famous for its 2010 eruption) to Seljalandsfoss waterfall — in January, the falls are often partially frozen, creating extraordinary ice formations. Walk behind the curtain of water (if ice conditions permit) for a unique perspective.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue east to Skógafoss waterfall — one of Iceland's largest and most photogenic falls, often adorned with ice crystals and rainbow mist in winter. Then visit the black sand beach at Reynisfjara — dramatic basalt column formations, roaring Atlantic waves, and the iconic Reynisdrangar sea stacks. Exercise extreme caution near the water (sneaker waves are dangerous). Continue to the Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon — a breathtaking lake filled with floating icebergs calved from Breiðamerkurjökull glacier, glowing blue and white in the winter light.
day_by_day.evening: Explore Diamond Beach adjacent to Jökulsárlón — where ice blocks wash ashore on the black sand, glittering like diamonds. Photograph the icebergs at dusk. Check into a premium guesthouse or hotel near Jökulsárlón (e.g., Fosshotel Glacier Lagoon or Hali Country Hotel) for the night.

meals.breakfast: Early breakfast at your Reykjavik hotel before the long drive.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Skógarfoss Café or a packed gourmet lunch from the hotel — eat with a view of the frozen waterfall.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Hali Country Hotel restaurant — a farm-to-table experience featuring local lamb, Arctic char from nearby rivers, and homemade Icelandic desserts. The hotel is owned by the family of celebrated Icelandic author Þórbergur Þórðarson.

day_by_day.notes: This is a very long driving day (~5–6 hours of driving plus stops) — depart by 7–8 AM to make the most of the limited daylight. The South Coast road can be icy and windy in January — studded tires and a 4WD vehicle are essential. Jökulsárlón is approximately 380 km from Reykjavik. Pre-book accommodation near the glacier lagoon well in advance.

day_by_day.morning: Skaftafell Glacier Hike on Vatnajökull — strap on crampons and harness up for a guided glacier hike on Europe's largest glacier. An expert glaciologist guide leads you across the ancient ice, through ice caves, past crevasses, and up to viewpoints with sweeping vistas of the surrounding volcanic landscape. Explore stunning blue ice formations and learn about the glacier's history and the effects of climate change. This is a world-class adventure experience.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Skaftafell area of Vatnajökull National Park — walk to Svartifoss waterfall, framed by dramatic hexagonal basalt columns that inspired the design of Hallgrímskirkja church in Reykjavik. The short hike through snow-covered birch forest is magical in winter. Then visit the Skaftafell Visitor Center to learn about the national park's extraordinary geology and ecology.
day_by_day.evening: Begin the drive back west along the South Coast toward Reykjavik, stopping at Vík í Mýrdal — Iceland's southernmost village, dramatically situated beneath the Mýrdalsjökull glacier. Check into a premium hotel in or near Vík (e.g., Black Beach Suites or Icelandair Hotel Vík) for the night. Scan the skies for aurora from the black sand beach.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at your Jökulsárlón area hotel before the glacier hike.
meals.lunch: Packed gourmet lunch on the glacier — the guide company typically provides hot soup in a thermos, sandwiches, and energy snacks. Eating lunch on a glacier is an unforgettable experience.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Suður-Vík Restaurant in Vík — a cozy, well-regarded restaurant serving fresh fish, Icelandic lamb, and homemade desserts with views of the dramatic coastline.

day_by_day.notes: Glacier hiking requires sturdy waterproof hiking boots (rentable on-site), warm layers, and waterproof outer clothing. The guide company provides crampons, ice axes, and helmets. Minimum fitness level required — the hike involves walking on uneven ice for 3–4 hours. Book the glacier hike well in advance as premium guided tours fill up quickly even in winter.

day_by_day.morning: Final morning — wake early for a last walk on Reynisfjara black sand beach near Vík as the sun rises (around 10:30 AM in January). The dramatic winter light, crashing waves, and basalt columns make for an unforgettable farewell to Iceland's wild south coast. Drive back toward Reykjavik and Keflavík, stopping at the Secret Lagoon Natural Hot Spring in Flúðir — Iceland's oldest swimming pool, a naturally heated geothermal pool surrounded by bubbling hot springs and geysers. Soak in the 38–40°C waters surrounded by steam and snow — a perfect final Icelandic experience.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue to Keflavík area. Stop in Reykjavik for last-minute shopping on Laugavegur — pick up premium Icelandic wool sweaters (lopapeysa), local design items, Icelandic spirits, and artisan chocolates. Visit the Kolaportið flea market (open weekends) or the Kringlan shopping mall for a wider selection. Head to Keflavík International Airport with ample time before departure.
day_by_day.evening: Departure from Keflavík International Airport. Relax in the Saga Lounge (Icelandair premium lounge) with a final Icelandic beer or glass of wine, reflecting on 13 extraordinary days in the land of fire and ice.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at your Vík hotel — fuel up for the final day of exploration.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Gamla Laugin (Secret Lagoon) café — warm soup and sandwiches after the hot spring soak, in a cozy wooden building.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at Apotek Restaurant in Reykjavik (if time permits before airport transfer) — a sophisticated brasserie in a historic pharmacy building, serving premium Icelandic seafood and meat dishes with an extensive cocktail menu. Alternatively, enjoy a final meal at the Saga Lounge at Keflavík Airport.

day_by_day.notes: The Secret Lagoon in Flúðir is approximately 1.5 hours from Vík and 1 hour from Keflavík — it fits perfectly into the final day's route. Pre-book entry online. Allow at least 3 hours at Keflavík Airport for international departure (security, duty-free, lounge time). Ensure all luggage is within airline weight limits — Icelandic wool purchases can be heavy! Consider shipping larger purchases home via the hotel concierge service.
